yarn.meaning: Every beat survives: the house-party, "Liberty Hall", eight and eight-twenty, the creak, Lorna Doone, the 1902 mandolin photo, the barges, the sonnets, the Alps inscription kept verbatim, Emerson, "Ten past nine, that's all!", skipping the bath.
yarn.sense: Mostly exact ("have a squiz at the pictures", "dodgy-looking barges", "Bit of a scruffy-looking lot"), but "open it, ever so politely" shifts "modestly" (discreetly) toward courtesy, and "Not bad, I s'pose" brings in a first-person narrator the second-person piece lacks.
yarn.authenticity: Natural: "Sleep in as long as you like", "kill a bit of time", "Oh, righto then!". "Some people _are_ like that. Too right they are." is a bolted-on tag.
yarn.register: Light level-2 touches ("brekkie", "beaut", "squiz", "dodgy") on a plain modern retelling; no swearing.
yarn.tone: The mock-solemn comedy of the anxious guest is intact: "Never touch a sonnet before breakfast", "We'll read it just to spite 'em."
yarn.flow: Reads smoothly; the added "Too right they are." after the italic punchline flattens it.
yarn.variety: Varied light slang with nothing leaned on: "brekkie", "beaut", "squiz", "dodgy", "righto", "on the sly", "a wander round".

unharnessed.meaning: All points kept, including the inscription verbatim and "Only ten past nine!".
unharnessed.sense: "perfectly bonzer" neatly replaces the American "perfectly bully"; "open it a modest crack", "scruffy-looking mob", "dodgy-looking barges" all fit.
unharnessed.authenticity: Natural throughout; "Scratch the bath as too noisy" is a slightly awkward hybrid of slang and the original's construction.
unharnessed.register: A light level-2 touch: "bonzer", "mob", "dodgy", "righto", "Sleep in"; no swearing.
unharnessed.tone: The dry, self-mocking comedy comes through whole: "Never touch a sonnet before breakfast", "We'll read it just out of spite."
unharnessed.flow: Reads like it was written that way.
unharnessed.variety: Modest but varied set; nothing repeated.

engine.meaning: Content largely unchanged, but the quoted inscription is altered to "To my beaut friends the Elbridges", which changes a quoted document.
engine.sense: "Too right, where there is a large house-party" uses an emphatic agreement for "Of course" as a discourse opener; "To my beaut friends" inserts slang into a 1907 inscription.
engine.authenticity: Slang words dropped into untouched period prose: "At what time is brekkie?", "Let's take a squiz", with American "perfectly bully" left in.
engine.register: Largely untranslated: three or four swapped words in the original's text, lighter than level 2.
engine.tone: The original tone mostly survives because the text is unchanged, but "To my beaut friends" jars the joke about the inscription.
engine.flow: Original text reads well, but "At what time is brekkie?" and "Too right, where there is" are jarring joins.
engine.variety: Only "Too right", "brekkie", "squiz", "beaut" in the whole piece.

yarn.quote: Some people _are_ like that. Too right they are.
yarn.why: Bolted-on tag that steps on the punchline.
Introduces an "I" voice into a piece written in "you".

unharnessed.original: Eliminate the tub as too noisy.
unharnessed.why: "Scratch ... as too noisy" is an awkward join.
"frightful" left as British period diction; fine but less Aussie.

engine.original: Of course, where there is a large house-party
engine.why: "Too right" is agreement, not a sentence opener meaning "of course".

engine.original: To my good friends the Elbridges

engine.original: The sentiment in this attitude is perfectly bully

summaries.yarn: A lively, natural level-2 retelling with good variety; a couple of small slips, including one bolted-on tag.
summaries.unharnessed: Faithful and smooth, with well-chosen light Aussie touches; the closest fit to a level-2 brief.
summaries.engine: A word-swap pass on the original that lands slang in the wrong places, including inside a quoted inscription.
